articles.title_orig: Live updates: SpaceX launches unprecedented test flight of massive Starship, aiming for orbit
articles.title_zh: Live updates: SpaceX launches unprecedented test flight of massive Starship, aiming for orbit
articles.content_orig:
• Liftoff successful: SpaceX’s Starship rocket, the most powerful rocket ever made, has launched from Starbase, Texas. The mission will seek to reach orbit for the first time during a 10-hour flight, deploying 26 operational Starlink satellites.
• What to expect: SpaceX will not attempt to land the Super Heavy rocket booster or return the upper Starship spacecraft to dry land. Both will aim for controlled splashdowns in the ocean.
• Coming up: SpaceX is facing intense pressure to get Starship ready for a crucial NASA test flight next year that could pave the way for the next moon landing.
You may have noticed that not all rocket-related headlines have been about the “ peaceful uses of outer space ” lately.
The United States recently revealed that it has deployed weapons into space for the first time, without saying what type of weapons or what they were intended to accomplish.
It’s only the latest in a long list of signs that space is rapidly becoming more militarized.
SpaceX has always played a massive role in supporting the United States’ strategic interests in orbit. The company famously once sued the US Air Force for the right to bid on rocket contracts ( and won ). The company now dominates the national security launch market.
And SpaceX’s space-based internet infrastructure has a national security bent of its own.
Starship’s task today was to deploy Starlink internet satellites that will help serve some of the company’s 12 million customers across 160 countries. But SpaceX is also using its space-based communications infrastructure to create a secure, military-grade network called Starshield for more than $6 billion.
Musk mentioned the secretive project during an August town hall, saying, “We can’t say too much about Starshield for obvious reasons — because it’s you know top secret and stuff — but the Starshield team has done amazing work, and it is now a vital part of America’s national security.”
The Department of War also recently announced it’s giving its workers access to Starshield AI’s Grok. (Grok, the AI model developed by xAI, is now part of SpaceX after a pre-IPO merger in February .)
Recent regulatory filings show that NASA administrator Jared Isaacman donated a whopping $3 million to President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. super Pac.
It’s a remarkably large donation and deeply unusual for a presidential appointee who is already confirmed to their post — espeicially a NASA appointee, as the space agency typically aims to position itself as apolitical.
NASA declined to comment on the donations, saying personal contributions fall outside the scope of the space agency’s communications duties. Isaacman told CNN that he has made “political and philanthropic donations” and declined to comment further on the matter.
Columbia law professor Richard Briffault, a campaign finance and government ethics expert, told CNN in an interview last week that there is nothing illegal about making such a donation — as unusual as it is. But it does raise ethics concerns, at least from an optics standpoint.
“It goes to the question of appearances: Is this an independent public servant serving the public interest, or is this somebody who is acting as a politician?” Briffault said.
This isn’t Isaacman’s first major donation to a Trump PAC. Last year, when Isaacman was attempting to get his nomination to lead NASA reinstated, he donated about $2 million to MAGA Inc. (Trump initially pulled the nomination, as CNN reported, because Isaacman had previously donated to Democrats. It was later reinstated, and Isaacman was confirmed in December.)
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has a preexisting relationship with Isaacman, as the Isaacman has paid SpaceX to fly him on two missions to orbit. Isaacman has repeatedly said he would not favor SpaceX in his official capacity.
Musk has also closely aligned himself with Trump and donated millions to MAGA Inc. But recently, Musk also expressed some regret about taking such a substantial role in campaigns.
“I got too involved in politics,” he told The Economist during a recent interview.
SpaceX will not allow Starship to stay in orbit for 10 hours, as the company had originally planned.
Mission controllers, during a recent “checkpoint” analysis, decided to end the mission a bit early.
Huot noted that Starship was able to deploy all 26 of its Starlink satellites and the company has made contact with each of them, marking a huge mission success. But it won’t complete quite as many laps of the planet at originally hoped for.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman chimed in on social media to congratulate SpaceX on its success so far, getting the upper Starship spacecraft, or “ship,” to orbit for the first time.
All 26 of SpaceX’s new Starlink V3 satellies are currently in orbit.
SpaceX already confirmed contact with at least some of them. There’s no word yet on the status of the satellites that were designed to also snap pictures of Starship’s heat shield as they flew away from the vehicle.
SpaceX has put a massive emphasis on studying and improving Starship’s heat shield. It’s designed to protect the vehicle as it makes the grueling journey back home, as diving back into Earth’s thick atmosphere can involve temperatures topping 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit.
Starship is currently in orbit, but SpaceX previously decided that it would reevaluate the flight plan every so often to ensure that things are safe and looking good. One of those checkpoints is coming up.
“We’ll get to that initial checkpoint at about one hour 28 minutes into the flight . That’s where the team can look at everything and decide: Do we need to come home early?” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said.
SpaceX can direct Starship to relight an engine and begin its trip home prematurely if anything goes wrong. That’s all designed to make sure Starship remains safe and does not lose control in orbit.
If SpaceX were to lose control of the vehicle as it is lapping the planet, it could remain stuck in orbit, posing a risk to active satellites.
SpaceX’s Starship conducted its 14th flight test on Monday, an unprecedented test flight to reach orbit.
Some of the 26 Starlink V3 satellites that Starship will deploy today are doing double duty: Before they go on to beam internet service to some of SpaceX’s 12 million internet customers, a few of these devices will play a role in researching how today’s test flight is going.
The heat shield is a vital component. It’s designed to protect the upper Starship spacecraft as it navigates the violent physics of reentering Earth’s thick inner atmosphere while traveling at speeds that can top 17,000 miles per hour.
And Starship’s heat shield doesn’t just have to work once. It has to work over and over and over again if SpaceX is going to realize its dream of rapidly reusing these rockets.
It’s perhaps one of the most daunting engineering challenges in a long list of technical quandaries that Starship is facing.
SpaceX confirmed it’s already made contact with the first Starlink V3 satellites after they were ejected from Starship’s cargo bay.
These are the first of a new generation of Starlinks that are intended to boost the network’s performance:
The Starship spacecraft has begun deploying its batch of 26 Starlink V3 satellites, the very first of a new generation of capacity-boosting Starlinks as SpaceX continues to build out its high-speed global internet business.
The Starlinks are designed to lie flat, stacked atop each other as they ride inside Starship’s cargo bay. They leave the vehicle by exiting through a narrow slat, sort of like a high-tech Pez dispenser.
One of Starship’s six engines just briefly reignited, as expected, and has officially sent the vehicle on a path to enter Earth orbit.
It’s a massive milestone. From here on out, Starship is traveling fast enough and at such a precise trajectory, that it’s begun falling around the planet.
Today’s test flight is expected to see Starship complete six full laps of Earth over about 10 hours.

Selling weapons to China is suddenly off the table. It’s unclear how it got on the table in the first place.
U.S. Ambassador David Perdue told Fox News Sunday that “President Trump continues to say: Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,” and that “he actually asked [Chinese] President Xi [Jinping] would he like to buy some at one point.”
But hours later, the Trump administration aggressively attempted to cover its own tracks. Two U.S. officials denied any such plan while speaking with The Wall Street Journal . One source told the daily that the White House had no intentions of selling weapons to Beijing, while the other acknowledged that it’s already illegal to do so. That ban circles back to Taiwan, which relies on U.S. weapons to deter Chinese encroachment.
China has reaffirmed for years that Taiwan is an inalienable part of its territory, and that it intends to formally reunite with the island nation. More than 23 million people live in Taiwan, and its sovereignty is highly contested due to a complex history of colonization.
The U.S. has provided material defense support to Taiwan since 1979, when Congress passed the Taiwan Relations Act. The law binds the U.S. to resist anything that would jeopardize Taiwan’s national security.
The White House rattled Beijing when it made an $11 billion arms sale to the island in December, with a separate $14 billion package expected down the line. Donald Trump has since held off on advancing that larger sale, despite urging from Senate Republicans ahead of Xi’s visit last week.
“It is difficult to imagine ​how the United States might credibly project influence deterrence in the Indo-Pacific if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances ​is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities,” Senators Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski, John Cornyn, and Thom Tillis wrote in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ahead of the state visit.
Trump has not commented on the abeyance since. However, Xi made his position regarding U.S. involvement in the region abundantly clear. On Thursday, Xi told Trump that he hoped America would take the “correct position” of opposing Taiwan’s independence.
Taiwanese Deputy Foreign Minister Francois Wu commented on the summit on Saturday, telling reporters in Taipei that maintaining military sales and providing Taiwan the support to defend itself was an “important U.S. interest” due to the island’s dominating semiconductor industry, reported Reuters .
Attorney General Todd Blanche crashed and burned while trying to defend President Donald Trump’s ever-increasing restrictions on the press.
Speaking on ABC’s This Week Sunday, Blanche struggled to keep his composure while facing questions about a federal judge’s temporary injunction on Trump’s decision to ban CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House.
Last week, a federal judge ruled that Trump’s decision had little to do with national security, as the Justice Department had argued in court, and that the president’s initial statements indicated that the ban stemmed from the media’s coverage of the Republican Party.
“Well, I’m not going to get into what the judge says, the litigation is ongoing. But our position has been clear from the beginning. What they say is exactly the issue when it comes to national security,” Blanche said.
When ABC host Martha Raddatz pressed him for a single example, Blanche appeared to claim that any negative reporting about the president was inaccurate.
“Give you an example of when CNN doesn’t report accurately? You cannot be asking me that!” Blanche said. “They don’t even disagree. There’s not even a real dispute that the information coming out of CNN and some of these other networks is wholly and completely, almost 100 percent, negative towards the president.”
Raddatz reminded Blanche that the judge ruled that the ban had nothing to do with national security, and the attorney general doubled down.
“At some point, the complete misinformation and the inaccuracy and the one-sided news out of certain organizations does become a national security issue and it’s not right for the people of the United States to have to put up with it,” Blanche said.
Blanche blew up when Raddatz asked whether the Trump administration planned to screen reporters.
“I did not say that! I did not say that! You don’t get to put words in my mouth! You don’t get to put words in my mouth! That’s not the way it works,” he cried.
Then Blanche balked at a question about what the First Amendment meant to him, and insisted that news coverage did not have to be positive for the Trump administration.
“But you heard what the president said: ‘They want to try to diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,’” Raddatz said.
“For you to pick out seven words and say, ‘Oh, that’s what the president means,’ that’s extraordinarily disingenuous,” Blanche said.
Clearly, the Trump administration simply can’t stand when the press reports on what the president actually says.
Despite the judge’s order, the Trump administration has continued to lash out at the press. Over the weekend, the president blocked CNN from traveling with him on Air Force One.
FBI Director Kash Patel appears to have spent his weekend schmoozing with a man his own department fired under suspicions of being a double agent in 2008.
Patel attended the wedding of former acting U.S. Attorney for New Jersey Alina Habba, who resigned in disgrace in December.
On Sunday, Israeli-born federal prosecutor Sigal Chattah shared a photo from the festivities, featuring herself, Habba, her new billionaire husband Turhan Mildon , and Ali Abdelaziz, a former UFC manager and NYPD and FBI informant suspected of being a double agent.
According to the 2013 book Enemies Within: Inside the NYPD’s Secret Spying Unit and bin Laden’s Final Plot Against America , Abdelaziz was initially hired by the NYPD to serve as a mole against Muslims of America, a Virginia-based group, but was dropped after they after administered a polygraph test and suspected he was a double agent. The FBI tried to deport him but was unable to, according to the book’s authors.
This is at least the second time Patel and Abdelaziz have been pictured together.
“Why, that’s Ali Abdelaziz is on the far left. Manages a lot of Russian, Belarusian and Chechen MMA fighters including Khamzat Chimaev, who is close to Kadyrov. Abdelaziz was an FBI informant until the Bureau dropped him because they suspected he was a double agent,” The Insider’s Michael Weiss wrote on X . “Looks like Ka$h (far right) has forgiven and forgotten. These MAGA weddings are Mos Eisley cantinas for counterintelligence.”
Patel also drew backlash for appearing with Chattah, who made headlines last year for allowing senior Israeli government official Tom Alexandrovich to return to Israel on bail after being arrested in a sting operation for soliciting sexual acts from a minor.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned that his country is “fully prepared for the war to be resumed” following President Trump’s threats to “annihilate” Iran during his U.N. General Assembly speech.
“We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war. It is up to President Trump to choose. He wanted unconditional surrender in the previous war in two days, and now, it is eight months they are fighting with no result. A new aggression would be certainly the same,” Araghchi said Sunday to Kristen Welker on NBC’s Meet the Press .

Everything old is new again as today Bose announced its first pair of wired earbuds since discontinuing the option in 2015. The new tethered earbuds, which are simply called the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds , do away with battery anxiety and the need to remember to charge them every few days. Their functionality is limited, but they do take advantage of the past 11 years of earbud innovation with the addition of active noise canceling.
The earbuds are available for preorder today through Bose’s online store for $99 in three color options: black, white smoke, and a “limited edition” green shade called dewdrop mint. While a release from the company says they’re expected to start shipping on October 15th, Bose’s online store says October 13th.
Two microphones on each earbud work alongside Bose’s QuietControl technology to deliver active noise canceling with multiple modes that can be cycled using a button on the headphone’s inline remote. Quiet Mode reduces the intensity of sounds around you while Aware Mode instead boosts them, but you can also turn off ANC entirely. There’s an additional microphone on the inline remote for making phone calls and it’s designed to effectively pick up your voice without having to be held close to your mouth.
Instead of a headphone connector on the end of the earbuds’ 4.2-foot cable you’ll find USB-C for connecting to smartphones and laptops with support for lossless audio with minimal latency. The earbuds also come with an IPX4 rating for water resistance so they can survive sweat, rain, and splashes but a complete dunking is a no-no. A zippered carrying case is included along with three sizes of silicone eartips and two sizes of stability wings that can provide a more secure fit during physical activities.

articles.content_orig:
China has ‘wiretapped the Red Sea,’ ex-White House official warns as satellite images reveal new spy hub ahead of Xi visit.
Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a dangerous surveillance hub, a former Pentagon official warned Sunday, after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint just six miles from a key $66 million-a-year U.S. military base in Djibouti, Africa.
The report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) cited new facilities which it said would likely enable the Chinese military to monitor activities of other militaries operating nearby, although it also clarified it was not possible to determine whether China was actively intercepting communications.
The developments, one defense expert told Fox News Digital, could also inject fresh tension into U.S.-China relations in the run-up to Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House on Sept. 24. Beijing's intelligence-gathering capabilities are already under renewed scrutiny.
"What China is clearly doing is building eavesdropping capabilities. That seems to be their aim," said Morgan Murphy , former Trump White House official and press secretary for Mark Esper when he was secretary of defense during the first Trump administration.
CHINA-LINKED SPY SITE EXPANSION IN CUBA RAISES ALARMS NEAR KEY US MILITARY BASES
Morgan Murphy said it was significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from America's base in Djibouti. ( STR/AFP via Getty Images)
"Beijing has clearly wiretapped the Red Sea. When you build a 30-meter (100-foot-wide) satellite dish and cover it with a dome, so nobody can see where it's pointing, it's pretty clear you're up to no good," Murphy added while stating of the Washington-based think tank, that "the specificity here reflects the thorough research we expect out of CSIS."
The report pinpoints a large southeastern facility showing a control building, three 30-meter dipole antennas for high-frequency communications, two smaller antennas for very and "ultra-high frequencies," three mobile satellite dishes, four probable 5G towers and what CSIS said was a "radome" covering an unidentified asset.
CSIS also highlighted two new communications facilities that it says have emerged since 2024 that are likely to form part of a C4ISR command architecture, expanding China’s ability to intercept signals, track naval movements and communicate with Beijing while monitoring foreign militaries in the region.
The facilities would provide China with "a much more robust picture of the operating environment in the region," the report said.
CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES
CSIS said commercial satellite imagery revealed that China’s military had installed new antennas, satellite communications equipment and signals intelligence assets at its base in Djibouti — its only formally acknowledged overseas military installation. (Planet Labs / Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS))
"This isn’t a supply depot — it’s a 50-yard line seat over America’s power projection and the U.S. Navy," Murphy said before stating that the U.S. has "128 bases in more than 51 countries — China has just one."
"But look at the location — a few miles from Camp Lemonnier, overlooking the choke point that moves roughly a sixth of global sea trade. Great powers don’t plant listening posts next to rival fleets for 'logistics,'" he warned.
"Britain held Gibraltar to see who entered the Med while Japan’s island radios came before the runways. The Soviets’ overseas sites were never just about fuel and Beijing is running that playbook on the Red Sea," Murphy added.
Although China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jian said China is "unaware of the specific situation" and framed the country as a "builder of international peace," the new facilities provide Beijing with a picture of regional operations, according to Reuters.
CHINA IS BUILDING A MASSIVE SHIP THAT SHOULD SCARE AMERICANS ABOUT THE FUTURE
Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a surveillance hub, former Pentagon officials warned after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint in Djibouti. ( DAPHNE BENOIT/AFP via Getty Images)
"The new report is helpful in framing the conversation, and it comes at an awkward time for China because Xi Jinping is visiting the White House on the 24th of this month," Murphy said.
"I'd bet a box of donuts this issue comes up. There is going to be public exposure of this, which Chinese leadership isn't used to. They aren't used to being asked tough questions by the press," he said.
President Donald Trump recently addressed Chinese intelligence efforts aboard Air Force One, acknowledging that China "spies on us" just as "we spy on them."
Trump's comments followed a report by The Wall Street Journal linking support from a Chinese entity to high-resolution satellite imagery used by Iran prior to a deadly missile attack on U.S. troops in Jordan.
"They basically do what we do," Trump noted, adding that "Xi has behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well. ... You know what they say? That China spies on us. I say you're right, and we spy on them, too," he said, according to Reuters .
RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER
President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of a bilateral meeting at Gimhae Air Base on Oct. 30, 2025 in Busan, South Korea. Trump said he wants to keep the Strait of Hormuz open in the Middle East for countries, including China. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Murphy noted, "Nations spy on each other — allies and adversaries alike."
"It is a very old playbook, and listening posts all over the world are typical of great powers, but where the metal hits the floorboard is when you try to use that information," he said before adding that China may "keep tabs on us, but they cannot project power like the United States can."
The proximity of China's facility to U.S. operations is a core concern. Located less than six miles from Camp Lemonnier — the primary U.S. counterterrorism hub in Africa — and near French, Italian and Japanese installations, the site has a history of friction with U.S. forces.
"We are just right around the corner from China, and yet it's not a cooperative relationship," Murphy explained.
"Back in 2018, they lasered two of our C-130 pilots' eyes who suffered lasting damage from that incident. Beijing denied it, of course, but we know the truth."
WE SHOULD USE REAGAN AS A GUIDE IN HANDLING OUR MODERN ARMS RACE WITH CHINA
U.S. military aircraft as seen at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti. Camp Lemonnier is the only permanent United States military base in Africa. (Getty Images)
During the 2018 incident , the Pentagon had formally complained to China after military-grade lasers were pointed at American pilots attempting to land at Camp Lemonnier, causing minor injuries.
While Beijing dismissed the allegations as "groundless accusations," the confrontation underscored the potential for friction between military forces operating from nearby bases.
"China has one overseas base. The United States has more than 128 — by some counts, over 700 installations around the world," Murphy said.
"So it's significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from ours in Djibouti. It is hugely strategically important, which is why, of course, we're there."
IS TRUMP CONSIDERING BOLD AFRICA PLAY TO PUSH BACK ON CHINA, RUSSIA AND ISLAMIC TERRORISTS?

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo Praises Europe’s Democracy, Diverging Once Again From Trump
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo Praises Europe’s Democracy, Diverging Once Again From Trump
articles.content_orig:
France may have a highly secularized culture, but it has given Pope Leo XIV a superstar welcome.
In Paris, around 800,000 lined the Champs-Élysées avenue, some waving Vatican or French flags while others climbed trees or stood on each other’s shoulders to get a glimpse of the popemobile. In Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, around 150,000 attended an open-air papal Mass, according to Vatican estimates which dwarf the numbers of faithful who turned out for the last papal visit in 2008.
During the four-day visit, Leo appeared comfortable and relaxed, delivering most of his speeches and reflections in French, as the Chicago-born pontiff sought to tackle several themes during the trip.
A strong focus of Leo’s has been on trying to revitalize faith in a traditional European Catholic heartland as well as on addressing the clerical sexual abuse scandal and big political topics such as artificial intelligence. He’s also offered some more personal, unscripted remarks, helping to shape a clearer picture of himself.
While his predecessor never made official visits to the major Catholic European countries of France and Spain, Pope Leo has traveled to both within the first year and a half since his election.
France is sometimes described as the “eldest daughter of the church” because of its deep Catholic roots, but it’s also faced a long-term trend of declining church attendance with estimates of just 5-8% of the population heading to the pews each week.
French bishops have more recently reported some good news though: a surprising rise in new church entrants after around 8,200 adolescents and 13,200 adults were baptized in 2026. That’s a 20% increase on the year prior, with the church also saying 42% of the adults seeking baptism are aged 18-25, a reflection of a trend showing Gen Z’s openness to religious faith .
It’s something Pope Leo will have noted at the Stade de France when 80,000 young people packed the venue for a jubilant – and loud – prayer vigil. It was similar to when the pontiff visited Spain in June.
“There is a quest for meaning. People need and are in search of meaning and answers to the big existential question,” Rev. Benoît Pouzin, a priest in southwest France involved in youth ministry, told CNN.
France has a strict separation between church and state, so each papal visit needs to be carefully navigated. But in a surprising twist, Leo’s Mass in Paris was celebrated on the Place de la Concorde, a site deeply linked to the secular Republic as it’s where the last king of France, Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined. The separation of the church started with the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution.
In another unusual move later in the trip, President Emmanuel Macron also attended a papal Mass in Metz, a city in the northeast, despite criticism in 2023 for doing the same during Pope Francis’ visit.
Many among the crowds also pointed to Leo’s role as the other major US leader on the world stage. It’s hard not to see him as a counterweight to President Donald Trump. In contrast to the Trump administration, the pope has called for stronger guardrails around the development of artificial intelligence, warning against a “paradise of machines” while in Paris.
The pope, who spoke out against the US war in Iran, also wants a more united Europe, a stronger European Union and stronger international cooperation. “Today, relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilized,” the pope said in Metz on Monday. “The value of keeping one’s word is dismissed; instead, people boast of lies and deceit.”
The pope’s speech also praised one of the founders of the European Union, Robert Schuman, for whom there is an ongoing formal cause to make him a saint.
On the papal plane, the American pontiff responded to Trump’s White House media ban, which includes CNN and other outlets. In answer to a question from CNN, he said he was “very happy that, here, you are all welcome and good coverage, I think, is very important and that we have it all the way around, for everyone.” The response was classic Leo: signaling his support for the press but not wishing to create an unnecessary dispute with the president.
The American pope’s in-flight interactions with journalists were rare, unscripted moments, with his answers often revealing more about his personality. On the flight from Rome to Paris, the pope was asked if he had anything to do with a miraculous recent Chicago White Sox victory, his beloved baseball team. “No comment,” he said before adding with a smile, “Great things happen in Chicago.”
He also recalled childhood memories of watching Fulton Sheen, the American archbishop and broadcaster who was recently declared “blessed,” one step ahead of sainthood, and revealed he’d been practising his French but was no longer using the Duolingo language app. “It’s fake news!” he said about recent reports. Leo has in the past been spotted using Duolingo to learn German.
Leo isn’t simply vocal about challenges of his homeland. He also voiced concern over assisted dying with France recently approving legislation granting the right to the incurably ill, which is strongly opposed by the Catholic Church. Leo spoke on the subject several times during his visit – most clearly in the “miracle shrine” town of Lourdes, known for drawing many sick and terminally ill pilgrims to its shrine.
The pope must, however, continue to wrestle with Catholic Church’s sexual abuse scandals. France was left shocked by a 2021 report that estimated around 330,000 children were sexually abused over 70 years by priests or other church figures. He addressed this by telling crowds the church must admit its own failings and heal “deep wounds” before holding a two-hour meeting with seven survivors of abuse.
The Vatican said that Leo thanked them “for their painful testimony” while “reaffirming his commitment to ensuring that the harm they suffered is not repeated for others.”
But the scandal still lingers. On the façade of the basilica in Lourdes, banners were placed over controversial mosaics ahead of Leo’s visit. These mosaics – which will now be covered indefinitely – were designed by a Slovenian priest and artist, Rev. Marko Rupnik, accused of sexual and psychological abuse of adult women. A local bishop said the pope backed how the apostolic nunciature was handling the artist’s works. Bishop Jean-Marc Micas also said Leo had ordered the Vatican’s in-house media outlets to stop using Rupnik art. Rupnik, who maintains his innocence, is facing a church trial in the Vatican, which complainants say is taking too long and lacks transparency.
The pope was elected 16-months ago and is still carving out a narrative for his papacy. Some in the Vatican find him difficult to read, and the pope is known for keeping his cards close to his chest. But it’s out on the open road when he travels abroad, in France and, in November, in Latin America, where the Leo papacy is beginning to take shape.
CNN’s Joseph Ataman contributed to this report.

The 2026 Major League Baseball postseason field has been set , and highest-of-high-stakes playoff baseball is upon us. To help set the scene for the month-long dramatics that will determine who wins both belt and title, we're here to rank the top players who will be participating in these playoffs. Specifically, we're about to rank the top 26 players chosen from the 12 teams making the 2026 postseason. So that's 26 in '26, you see.
As for the criteria, excellence in the current season and whether or not said excellence seems sustainable in the near term are the leading considerations. It's also about the current value at this moment in time. Effectively, that means players whose "counting stats" may have taken a hit because of injury earlier in the season but are now healthy and in prime form will be on here despite some cumulative deficits. As such, these rankings are more about who's primed and skilled enough to put up big numbers in October (and possibly November).
On that point, it's worth noting that a handful of elite performers on these 12 teams won't be here because of current injury woes. Most notably, Yankees slugger and back-to-back American League MVP Aaron Judge will not be ranked. Under normal circumstances, he'd be near the top of the stack, but he's on the injured list with a calf strain and may not be able to play in the Yankees' Wild Card Series clash with the rival Red Sox . As such, Judge's spot in the rankings to come will have to go to someone else.
Now let's get to the rankings. Given that we're talking about just 26 players from the 12 best teams, the bar is quite high, and painful omissions were abundant. Onward …
It's a 40-homer season and another round of high-level durability for the stalwart first baseman. Olson's been one of the steadiest power producers in the game over the last decade, and his spot here is much deserved.
The 34-year-old Contreras, now a first baseman, has put up a career year at the plate in his first season with the Red Sox. He leads the team in homers, has a high OBP, and boasts an OPS+ north of 150. That's a true middle-of-the-order force.
Henderson spent most of the early weeks of the season in Triple-A and then missed significant time with a back strain. Since early July, though, he's been a force in the Milwaukee rotation. He's thrived at the run-prevention and command-and-control level across his 2026 starts, and at age 24, there's more to come.
The affable rookie lefty has a strong body of work overall across 26 starts, and he enters the postseason on a particular roll. Since the start of August, Tolle has a 2.52 ERA and an even better FIP, and he's struck out a hefty 31.8% of opposing batters. He's in ace form at the right time.
A pending free agent, Suzuki picked an opportune time for a career year. He's topped 5.0 WAR for the first time in MLB , and in related matters, he's thrived in the field and at the plate. On the latter point, Suzuki heads into the playoffs with 26 home runs and 81 walks.
Some of the shine has come off Rice in the second half, but overall, he's put up a stellar season in 2026. The 27-year-old All-Star has mashed right-handed pitching, and he's third in the American League in home runs and 10th in times on base. Rice has been a vital presence in the Yankee lineup with Aaron Judge missing so much time.
Wheeler, who's been an ace for years on Philly's watch, came up big in the must-win Game 162, which is what he's done all season. In 162 innings, he allowed 55 runs with 193 strikeouts and 47 walks. That's a heck of a season for a 36-year-old coming off surgery to correct thoracic outlet syndrome.
Laudably, Bregman made it back into the Cubs ' lineup mere days after suffering facial fractures. Now he's set to resume being a quality hitter at the plate and in the field, a key part of the best team defense in all of baseball. This season, the veteran infielder boasts 26 homers and 75 walks.
A full-time DH with a low batting average? That's one way to look at Schwarber. Another way is as the MLB home run leader who's drawn more than 100 walks on the season. It's the latter set of characteristics that matter more, so consider him to be one of the best "take and rake" hitters around.
The underrated and overlooked Rasmussen has been stellar in his age-30 campaign. He's set career-best marks in innings, strikeouts, ERA, FIP, and ERA+. He's been an ace in each of the last two seasons, and in 2026, he's been one of the best starting pitchers around.
The top rookie pitcher in all of baseball this season, Messick has been an essential presence for the AL Central champs. Across a hefty 186 ⅓ innings this season, Messick had an ERA of 2.56 with 193 strikeouts and a WAR of more than 6.0. That'll do, P-Mess. That'll do.
Harris, who's still just 25 years of age, has been a standout defensive center fielder this season. At the plate, he's also thrived, as he's slugged .491 with 63 extra-base hits and good speed on the bases.
The prime mover for the upstart White Sox broke out in a big way this season. Across more than 700 plate appearances, the 26-year-old corner infielder surpassed 5.0 WAR and 100 walks while also smacking 33 homers and stealing 22 bases in 24 attempts.
Tatis suffered some brutal luck on batted balls early in the season, but the quality of contact was always there. In the second half, the Padres ' superstar has found his expected level in a major way, which means he's in peak form heading into the playoffs.
We all think a lot of Fried as a pitcher, but is he still underrated? He boasts a stellar ERA+ of 142 for his career, and this season he's been even better on a rate basis. He's backed it up with a 2.65 FIP over 20 starts. Elbow issues compromised his innings load in 2026, but he's been in peak form in September for the most part.
The 22-year-old phenom has put together his strongest season yet. He boasts excellent defense in left, and at the plate, he's put up an OPS+ of 127 to go with a 20-20 campaign. All of that's been good for a WAR of almost 5.0.
Since arriving in MLB prior to the 2024 season, Yamamoto has done nothing but pitch like an ace. This year, the 28-year-old right-hander has been even better than he was in 2025, when he finished third in the National League Cy Young vote. He's been the rotation bedrock for LA.
Turang has for some time been one of the top defensive second basemen around, and over the last two seasons, he's stepped up his game at the plate in a major way. All of that plus speed on the bases make Turang one of the most underrated players in MLB today. But he's not underrated in these rankings.
Ohtani made it back into the Dodgers ' lineup before the end of the regular season, but his ongoing knee issues cast some doubt over his postseason outlook. He said late in the year that he wouldn't pitch for the rest of the season, which presumably includes the playoffs, and it's possible he's compromised at the plate to some extent. That said, a compromised Ohtani who doesn't pitch at all is still better than, oh, almost every other player around.
At an age when most pitchers are in deep decline or out of the league entirely, Sale just keeps getting better. Boasting the best fastball velocity of his career, Sale in 2026 put up an ERA+ of 195 and led the majors in K/BB ratio.
In a Jacob Misiorowski-less universe, Sánchez would be the NL Cy Young winner thanks to his across-the-board excellence this season. He's topped 200 innings for a second straight season, he's logged a sub-3.00 ERA (and an even better FIP), and he has a K/BB ratio of more than 5.00. That's an ace, and this isn't his first time pitching like one.

articles.title_orig: Leo’s visit across France offers a more personal glimpse of the pope
articles.title_zh: Leo’s visit across France offers a more personal glimpse of the pope
articles.content_orig:
France may have a highly secularized culture, but it has given Pope Leo XIV a superstar welcome.
In Paris, around 800,000 lined the Champs-Élysées avenue, some waving Vatican or French flags while others climbed trees or stood on each other’s shoulders to get a glimpse of the popemobile. In Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, around 150,000 attended an open-air papal Mass, according to Vatican estimates which dwarf the numbers of faithful who turned out for the last papal visit in 2008.
During the four-day visit, Leo appeared comfortable and relaxed, delivering most of his speeches and reflections in French, as the Chicago-born pontiff sought to tackle several themes during the trip.
A strong focus of Leo’s has been on trying to revitalize faith in a traditional European Catholic heartland as well as on addressing the clerical sexual abuse scandal and big political topics such as artificial intelligence. He’s also offered some more personal, unscripted remarks, helping to shape a clearer picture of himself.
While his predecessor never made official visits to the major Catholic European countries of France and Spain, Pope Leo has traveled to both within the first year and a half since his election.
France is sometimes described as the “eldest daughter of the church” because of its deep Catholic roots, but it’s also faced a long-term trend of declining church attendance with estimates of just 5-8% of the population heading to the pews each week.
French bishops have more recently reported some good news though: a surprising rise in new church entrants after around 8,200 adolescents and 13,200 adults were baptized in 2026. That’s a 20% increase on the year prior, with the church also saying 42% of the adults seeking baptism are aged 18-25, a reflection of a trend showing Gen Z’s openness to religious faith .
It’s something Pope Leo will have noted at the Stade de France when 80,000 young people packed the venue for a jubilant – and loud – prayer vigil. It was similar to when the pontiff visited Spain in June.
“There is a quest for meaning. People need and are in search of meaning and answers to the big existential question,” Rev. Benoît Pouzin, a priest in southwest France involved in youth ministry, told CNN.
France has a strict separation between church and state, so each papal visit needs to be carefully navigated. But in a surprising twist, Leo’s Mass in Paris was celebrated on the Place de la Concorde, a site deeply linked to the secular Republic as it’s where the last king of France, Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined. The separation of the church started with the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution.
In another unusual move later in the trip, President Emmanuel Macron also attended a papal Mass in Metz, a city in the northeast, despite criticism in 2023 for doing the same during Pope Francis’ visit.
Many among the crowds also pointed to Leo’s role as the other major US leader on the world stage. It’s hard not to see him as a counterweight to President Donald Trump. In contrast to the Trump administration, the pope has called for stronger guardrails around the development of artificial intelligence, warning against a “paradise of machines” while in Paris.
Pope Leo said he is taking the warnings about Artificial Intelligence’s threat to humanity seriously, and said it is irresponsible for people to sit back and dismiss the risks of AI.
Trump has dismissed the warnings about AI as a “hoax” which he made during a surprise phone call with Jensen Huang, the CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, at a summit in Los Angeles.
“I don’t think that that is fake news – as some have said – to try and pause,” Leo XIV said on board the papal plane from Metz to Rome.
Leo, who has expressed a keen interest in artificial intelligence since the start of his papacy, said that he found it “interesting” that Huang had unveiled a new tool to prevent AI agents from operating out of human control.
“He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation,” the Pope said.
The pope devoted his first major theological document to AI earlier this year, warning about the use of AI in warfare and calling for stronger ethical foundation to the development of the technology.
The pope explained that the Vatican had established its own AI commission to understand how to use it, along with the risks and benefits, and that “we need to continue to invite political leaders, the leaders of AI” so they can “look at what is happening already and what could be down the road.”
He explained: “We are trying to continue to promote dialog, study, investigation, to find ways to make sure that AI does not get to a point where it could destroy humanity.”
“If someone were to ask me, am I in panic mode? No, I’m not, I sleep at night” the pope said, but added: “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously.”
“To simply say, oh, it’s not going to happen and close our eyes to it, I think, is probably not the most responsible way to go about that,” Leo said.
The pope, who spoke out against the US war in Iran, also wants a more united Europe, a stronger European Union and stronger international cooperation. “Today, relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilized,” the pope said in Metz on Monday. “The value of keeping one’s word is dismissed; instead, people boast of lies and deceit.”
The pope’s speech also praised one of the founders of the European Union, Robert Schuman, for whom there is an ongoing formal cause to make a saint.
Pope Leo XIV has warned against the use of Christianity by far-right political groups, while calling on the church to be active in seeking to prevent extremism. Speaking on board the papal plane, he said that “the combination of these far-right points of view with a certain kind of religion” cannot be considered an “authentic expression of Christianity.”
The pope’s comments came in response to a question about the rise of extremist parties in Germany as he flew back from making a major speech on European Unity at the French-German border.
“We go back to the values of the Gospel [Christian teaching], which are not about hatred and division, but they’re about understanding and compassion,” the pope said.
The American pontiff also responded to Trump’s White House media ban, which includes CNN and other outlets. In answer to a question from CNN, he said he was “very happy that, here, you are all welcome and good coverage, I think, is very important and that we have it all the way around, for everyone.” The response was classic Leo: signaling his support for the press but not wishing to create an unnecessary dispute with the president.
The American pope’s in-flight interactions with journalists were rare, unscripted moments, with his answers often revealing more about his personality. On the flight from Rome to Paris, the pope was asked if he had anything to do with a miraculous recent Chicago White Sox victory, his beloved baseball team. “No comment,” he said before adding with a smile, “Great things happen in Chicago.”
He also recalled childhood memories of watching Fulton Sheen, the American archbishop and broadcaster who was recently declared “blessed,” one step ahead of sainthood, and revealed he’d been practicing his French but was no longer using the Duolingo language app. “It’s fake news!” he said about recent reports. Leo has in the past been spotted using Duolingo to learn German.
Leo isn’t simply vocal about challenges of his homeland. He also voiced concern over assisted dying with France recently approving legislation granting the right to the incurably ill, which is strongly opposed by the Catholic Church. Leo spoke on the subject several times during his visit – most clearly in the “miracle shrine” town of Lourdes, known for drawing many sick and terminally ill pilgrims to its shrine.

articles.title_orig: Robert Pattinson’s Star Power and Gen Z: 5 Reasons ‘Primetime’ Became a Breakout Box Office Hit
articles.title_zh: Robert Pattinson’s Star Power and Gen Z: 5 Reasons ‘Primetime’ Became a Breakout Box Office Hit
articles.content_orig:
Senior Film and Media Reporter
Plenty of moviegoers had a seat for “ Primetime ,” a true-crime thriller starring Robert Pattinson as Dateline NBC journalist and “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen.
The A24 movie landed on the higher end of box office expectations, scoring $19.2 million from 2,863 North American venues in its opening weekend. Although “Primetime” ranked in fourth place on domestic charts — behind Disney’s “Avengers: Endgame Encore” ($26 million), Sony’s “Resident Evil” reboot ($23 million) and fellow newcomer, Paramount’s wilderness adventure “The Heart of the Beast” ($20 million) — it cost just $15 million to produce and is already well-positioned to turn a profit theatrically.
Notably, “Primetime” marks the third-best opening weekend ever for A24, behind this summer’s sleeper hit “Backrooms” ($81.4 million) and Alex Garland’s 2024 dystopian “Civil War” ($25.5 million) and, impressively, above Josh Safdie and Timothée Chalamet’s 2025 ping-pong drama “Marty Supreme” ($15.7 million). This is Pattinson’s second consecutive hit with A24 following this spring’s dark relationship dramedy “The Drama,” which co-starred Zendaya and opened to $14.3 million domestically.
Directed by Lance Oppenheim, “Primetime” revolves around the production of “To Catch a Predator” and Hansen’s increasingly frenetic attempts to confront child sexual predators in complex sting operations. Critics embraced the movie, which holds an 87% on Rotten Tomatoes. Moviegoers gave “Primetime” a mixed “B” grade on CinemaScore exit polls, which isn’t all that surprising given the film’s intentionally unsettling nature.
“Considering the tough subject material, the audience score is good,” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “This is a hit.”
Here are five reasons “Primetime” was, well, ready for primetime at the box office.
It’s been a big year for Pattinson, the “Twilight” heartthrob-turned-bona-fide movie star. In 2026, he’s been in “The Drama,” Christopher Nolan’s summer smash “The Odyssey” and will appear in the upcoming sci-fi sequel “Dune: Part III.” While he shares the credit with Zendaya and Nolan for those wins, Pattinson is undeniably the draw in “Primetime.” More than 75% of audiences cited Pattinson as their No. 1 reason for buying a ticket, according to exit polls from PostTrak. What’s more impressive is Pattinson managed to get people to theaters without too splashy a press tour. (In addition to starring in just about every movie this year, he’s been busy filming “The Batman: Part II” in London.) He didn’t scale the Sphere in Las Vegas or advertise on blimps to get out the word about “Primetime.” Pattinson showed up at Venice Film Festival, where “Primetime” bowed to raves, and participated in some phone interviews . But otherwise, he let the movie do the talking.
Opening weekend crowds for “Primetime” skewed heavily Gen Z, with 69% of audiences under the age of 30. That’s especially significant because most Zoomers were way too young to watch “To Catch a Predator” when the show aired from 2004-2007. It helped that “Primetime” tapped into their love for the true-crime genre. The turnout also highlighted the audience that A24 has cultivated over the years, thanks to edgy, aesthetic and conversation-starting arthouse favorites like “Marty Supreme,” “Lady Bird,” “Everything Everywhere All at Once” and more. “Primetime” is the indie studio’s second release of the year to become a full-fledged event for younger moviegoers. The first was “Backrooms,” which became a wildly profitable breakout sensation with $400 million against a $10 million budget. It’s all a huge relief to theater owners, who worried that younger generations viewed the big screen as outdated.
Pattinson, meanwhile, might credit the win to Gen Z supporting their own. Pattinson has joked that he’s Gen Z (despite being 40, which makes him squarely a Millennial). During Vanity Fair’s Lie Detector test , his “Die My Love” co-star Jennifer Lawrence hilariously accused Pattinson of thinking he’s Gen Z because he likes to cold-call people on FaceTime. He claimed his birth year “doesn’t matter,” to which she replied, “I believe that you believe you’re Gen Z.”
A24 ran an effective social media-heavy campaign for “Primetime.” But whether he intended to or not, the real-life Hansen also stoked a ton of interest by continuously speaking out against the movie. Way before he got to see the film, Hansen was vocal in his criticism about Pattinson’s “overly dramatic” portrayal of him. He also stressed that “Primetime” isn’t a literal account of his career and questioned the studio’s “motive” in dramatizing the making of the hit reality series. When Hansen finally watched “Primetime,” he wasn’t all that enthused . He called the film “so bizarre” and “detached from reality.” In the process, he made plenty of headlines and put “Primetime” on the radar of “To Catch a Predator” fans across the country.
The Venice Film Festival can be hit or miss in terms of launching a movie into the mainstream. For every critical and commercial success like “A Star Is Born,” “The Shape of Water” and “La La Land,” there’s a high-profile misfire à la “Joker: Folie à Deux” or “After the Hunt.” Venice worked as the kickoff for “Primetime,” which was embraced with an enthusiastic seven-minute standing ovation . Since there weren’t many Hollywood-backed movies at the glamorous Italian festival, “Primetime” became the talk of Lido — leading to weeks of positive world-of-mouth before general audiences saw the film. That’s amore!
Oppenheim, the 30-year-old filmmaker known for documentaries like “Some Kind of Heaven” and HBO’s “Ren Faire,” was already emerging as a major emerging talent after “Primetime,” his narrative feature debut. And then, just days after “Primetime” launched at Venice, Oppenheim reached a new level of fame after he and comedian Nathan Fielder unveiled their top-secret documentary “You Can See Everything,” about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, at Telluride Film Festival . Seemingly overnight, Oppenheim found himself on everyone’s radar, which brought even more eyes to this project. Call it the Elizabeth Holmes bump?

articles.title_orig: White House releases new taxpayer-funded ad describing ‘final battle’
articles.title_zh: White House releases new taxpayer-funded ad describing ‘final battle’
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration put out a new ad this weekend as part of its “PSA” campaign, this time showing President Donald Trump walking down a hallway as he asks people to join him in his fight to “expel the warmongers from our government.”
The ad — which at the end says it was “Paid for by the U.S. government” — is nearly identical to an ad put out by Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.
Trump posted that ad to Truth Social in January 2024. The repurposed ad now includes “Paid for by the U.S. government.” But it excludes the last few seconds of the 2024 ad, which ends with text reading “Join President Trump’s fight to save America” and his 2024 campaign logo.
The ad signals an expansion of the White House’s controversial use of government funds to air pieces that resemble campaign advertisements. Last week, the White House ran a television ad in which Trump described how he wanted to “defeat communism,” set to the song “Love Me” by JMSN . The White House has called the ads “public service announcements.”
In the latest ad, dramatic black-and-white video shows President Trump walking down a hallway with audio of him saying it is the “final battle” and vowing to “demolish the deep state” and “throw off the sick political class that hates our country.”
“We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” it concludes.
Federal law requires political advertisers to submit certain public disclosures and generally bans using public funds for political advertising. Since the administration maintains the ads are public service announcements, it’s not clear whether those disclosures are available. The White House has not released a specific source of government funding used to air the ads.
AdImpact, a political ad tracking firm, has estimated that the administration has spent more than $1.7 million to run these ads, which have been running heavily in recent days during prominent television programming like football games, Sunday morning news shows, and prime time broadcast shows. That said, AdImpact doesn’t have full visibility into airings on every cable channel in every market in the country, hampering that estimate.
The White House defended the ad Sunday, pointing NBC News to a statement it had offered last week when it commented on the other ads released by the administration.
“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad. The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country,” a White House spokesperson said.
Another White House official pushed back on the line of questioning: “The PSAs are clearly not political. The president is not on the ballot, and the ads don’t have a call to action.”
The White House did not specifically respond to NBC News’ question about the ad’s being nearly identical to the 2024 Trump campaign ad.
A White House spokesperson also pointed to past examples of ads released by former administrations, including an ad by George W. Bush’s Department of Health and Human Services, a social media campaign by Barack Obama’s Environmental Protection Agency in 2014 and 2015 and an effort by Joe Biden’s administration encouraging Covid-19 vaccination.
The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office dinged the Bush and Obama ad campaigns — Bush’s for not properly disclosing the government was the source and Obama’s for violating “publicity or propaganda and anti-lobbying provisions.”
White House communications director Steven Cheung defended the recent pro-Trump ads Sunday on social media , writing, “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv.”
CNN and The New York Times were first to report about the ad’s being almost identical to Trump’s 2024 campaign ad.
Spending taxpayer dollars on the ads has raised legal and ethical concerns and condemnation from both parties.
“This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and utterly illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars,” congressional Democratic appropriators wrote in a letter Friday addressed to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.
The letter was signed by Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash.; Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I.; Rep. Rosa De Lauro, D-Conn.; and Rep. Steny Hoyer, D-Md.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said Sunday in an interview with CBS that public officials should not “spend public money on private ads for themselves.”
Megan Shannon is an Associate Producer for the White House Unit.
Garrett Haake is NBC News' chief White House correspondent.
Raquel Coronell Uribe is a politics reporter for NBC News.

In a Fox News Digital exclusive, Finnish President Alexander Stubb discusses efforts to end the war in Ukraine, pushes back on fears of a Russian attack on Finland and addresses growing military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran.
UNITED NATIONS — As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Russia could take its war beyond Ukraine, Finnish President Alexander Stubb is striking a markedly calmer tone — saying Finland is prepared for Moscow and crediting President Donald Trump with pushing harder for a negotiated end to the war.
"I think we're certainly in a better place than we were before President Trump started," Stubb told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. "He's doubled down in the past year and a half to try to find a solution for peace with negotiators such as Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and many others."
Stubb, who has been closely involved in the diplomatic effort, said he and Norway’s prime minister have worked largely "in the back office," relaying information among Ukraine, the United States and European governments.
KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE
US President Donald Trump meets with Finnish President Alexander Stubb in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 9, 2025. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP) (Photo by JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images) (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)
"I think he's really working hard and hopefully we'll get a solution," Stubb said.
The interview came during an intense diplomatic week in New York focused heavily on the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in New York during UNGA week as Washington continued its effort to revive negotiations with Moscow. Zelenskyy said peace remained Ukraine's priority and thanked Trump for sending the two envoys to Kyiv after they had also held talks in Moscow.
Zelenskyy was asked by Fox News Digital after the meeting about the possibility that Russia could invade or attack another European country in the near future.
BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine's president, left, and Alexander Stubb, Finland's president, right, during a news conference in Helsinki, Finland, on Wednesday, March 19, 2025. (Roni Rekomaa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"That's why the risk of offensive by drones, missiles or land operation is very high against other countries who are bordering Russia or Belarus ," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin , unable to achieve his military objectives in Ukraine, could seek to create instability elsewhere in Europe to pressure Western governments into reducing their support for Kyiv. He pointed to drone incursions and disruptions affecting several European countries, arguing that Moscow is already attempting to intimidate European societies and test their response.
Asked by Fox News Digital what European countries should do in response to the growing threat, Zelenskyy offered a direct answer.
"Respond. Always respond. It's not about the war. If you don't respond, Russians, they will go further," he said.
But Stubb struck a notably calmer tone when asked about Zelenskyy’s warnings that Russia could eventually attack other European countries, including Finland, which shares the longest border with Russia.
"As commander-in-chief in Finland, I sit on all the relevant information and I just don't see a factual basis for it," Stubb said.
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT
Commander of the Finnish Army Lieutenant General Pasi Valimaki addresses Finnish conscript soldiers after a military exercise at Pori Brigade in Niinisalo, Finland, Dec. 9, 2025. (Anne Kauranen/Reuters)
That does not mean, he stressed, that Moscow has stopped targeting Europe.
Stubb distinguished between the "kinetic" war Russia is fighting in Ukraine and what he described as a broader "hybrid" campaign in Europe, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea.
"We have to see this as a campaign," he said. "Russia tries to intimidate Europe, scare us and get into our heads."
His prescription was characteristically Finnish: "cool, calm and collected, take a sauna and a nice bath and deal with it."
Stubb said Finland, a country with a population of 5.6 million, can afford that attitude precisely because it has spent decades preparing for a potential threat from its eastern neighbor.
"We are calm because we are prepared," he said.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb answers questions during an exclusive Fox News Digital interview in New York City. (Brooke Curto / Fox News Digital)
He pointed to Finland’s mandatory military service, reserve force, artillery, long-range capabilities and extensive network of civilian shelters. The Finnish Defence Forces puts Finland’s wartime military strength at 280,000 personnel, with additional reservists available if needed.
That deterrent received another boost just days before Stubb traveled to New York. Finland is acquiring 64 F-35A fighter jets to replace its F/A-18 Hornet fleet under a procurement decision announced by the Finnish government.
The first two F-35s intended for operations inside Finland arrived at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, according to a Finnish Defence Forces press release.
"We have obligatory military service. I did mine, my son did his. We have women who do it voluntarily. We have over 60 F-18s. We just bought 64 F-35s, the two first of which arrived. We have long-range missiles, air, land and sea. We have the capability to mobilize 280,000 troops within days in a conflictual situation. On top of that, we have land mines. And we have the biggest artillery in Europe together with Poland… On top of that, we have civilian shelters for over 4.4 million people out of 5.6."

Security cameras overlook the Niirala Border Crossing Station along Finland's eastern border with Russia in Nov. 2023 after Finland closed the checkpoint amid heightened border security concerns. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)
"We don't have them because we're worried about Sweden," Stubb joked of Finland’s military capabilities. "We have them because we see a security threat coming from Russia."
He said that level of preparedness, combined with Finland’s NATO membership, makes a direct Russian attack unlikely. Finland became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, after abandoning its longstanding military non-alignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"We feel that we're very prepared, and that gives us a strong enough … deterrent that we don't believe that Russia is going to test a country like Finland," Stubb said. "And of course the icing on the cake is that we are now security providers in the Alliance NATO."
Stubb also used his Sept. 22 address to the U.N. General Assembly to advocate for continued support for Kyiv, calling the "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine "particularly close to my heart." He said the coalition was working toward a "just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the U.N. Charter."
Stubb made additional news on Ukraine during UNGA week, when he urged SpaceX owner Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage so Ukrainian forces could use the satellite network in areas containing Russian ballistic missile launchers , including inside Russia. He argued that doing so could help Ukraine target launchers firing missiles at Ukrainian cities.
Yet Ukraine was only one piece of what Stubb described as an increasingly interconnected global security crisis.

Nvidia is launching a new safety platform designed to contain and monitor AI agents, a move that comes in response to a wave of rogue hacking incidents , as reported earlier by Reuters . In an announcement on Monday , Nvidia says its new Open Agent Safety Platform can quarantine agents that attempt to escape their boundaries within “milliseconds.”
The platform uses Nvidia’s OpenShell open-source software, which runs on the company’s Vera AI CPU . Users can choose the information an AI agent can access, and OpenShell checks these restrictions before and during a task, according to Nvidia . It also includes Nvidia’s Sentry technology on a separate chip to continuously monitor agents and enforce boundaries.
During an interview with CNBC , Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang emphasized the importance of giving AI agents access to only the information they need to do their job. “In order for you to deliver that agentic system in a safe way, you have to make sure that the sandbox around it… all of those systems are designed in a way that keeps the agent with minimal rights,” Huang said.
Concerns about AI safety have risen in recent weeks , as OpenAI , Anthropic , and Google have all revealed incidents where their AI models went outside their testing environments and hacked other companies. Several major tech companies are backing Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform, including Anthropic, Microsoft, and SpaceX.

articles.title_orig: Africa’s most visited country may have again granted visa access to one of the biggest sources of tension between China and the US
articles.title_zh: Africa’s most visited country may have again granted visa access to one of the biggest sources of tension between China and the US
articles.content_orig:
Two months after suspending the tourist visa application process for Taiwanese nationals, the Kingdom of Morocco reversed its decision last week, allowing people from the Asian country to reapply for visas.
Back in July, the Moroccan government directed its embassies and consulates globally to stop processing visa confirmation letters for Taiwanese nationals.
DON'T MISS THIS: 3 African nations revoke airspace access, forcing Taiwan president to cancel Africa trip
Prior to the suspension, Taiwanese nationals traveling to Morocco for commercial or tourism purposes were required to secure a visa confirmation letter, as reported by Taiwan’s Bureau of Consular Affairs.
Applications were formally submitted via the Moroccan Embassy in Japan and transmitted to the relevant authorities in Rabat for evaluation, following which approved applicants received authorization to obtain a visa upon arrival at a Moroccan airport.
However, Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs indicated that the embassy informed travel agencies on July 23 of the cessation of new application processing, per the directive issued to Moroccan diplomatic missions worldwide.
Shortly after Morocco’s decision, Taiwan responded, issuing a visa ban of its own to the North African country under a policy it described as the principle of reciprocity.
These decisions signaled a diplomatic rift between both nations, as no clear explanation was given for Morocco’s visa ban.
Currently, Morocco has gone back on its July decision, as it is now allowing people from Taiwan to apply for tourism visas again, per information from the Taiwanese government.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) told CNA that its office in Tokyo contacted the Moroccan Embassy in Japan on Friday and was informed that applications for Visa Confirmation Letters (VCLs) had reopened on September 21.
However, Morocco is still not processing VCL applications for Taiwanese visitors travelling for purposes other than tourism.
Taiwan said it would continue to reject visa applications from Moroccan nationals until the remaining restrictions are lifted, as seen on Focus Taiwan .
Morocco is hardly the only African country Taiwan is having travel complications with, as it recently had the East African country of Uganda in focus too.
In August, Taiwan issued a travel advisory warning its citizens against visiting Uganda following reports that authorities there had confiscated passports and demanded Chinese documentation, further intensifying diplomatic friction surrounding Beijing’s policy.
The advisory came after three Taiwanese business travellers and their family members arrived at Entebbe International Airport near Kampala.
According to Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ugandan immigration officials seized their Taiwanese passports and demanded that they present Chinese passports instead.
The documents were eventually returned, and the travellers were allowed into Uganda.
However, Taiwan said the incident was the second recent case involving its citizens.
In the earlier case, two Taiwanese travellers encountered similar problems, with one eventually deported from the country.
According to Taiwan’s foreign ministry, Ugandan officials said the passport requirement was linked to the country’s “one-China policy,” which recognises Beijing’s position that Taiwan is part of China.
Taiwan has a limited diplomatic footprint in Africa, largely because most countries on the continent recognise Beijing under the One-China policy.
The African Union reaffirmed its support for the policy in January 2026, recognising the People’s Republic of China as the sole legal government representing China and backing Beijing’s position that Taiwan is part of China.
However, Eswatini remains the only African country with formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, while the continent’s other countries maintain relations with Beijing.
In April, Taiwan accused China of attempting to disrupt President Lai Ching-te’s planned visit to Eswatini by pressuring neighbouring countries to withdraw overflight permissions.
Lai's visit, originally scheduled for April 22–26 to mark the 40th anniversary of King Mswati III’s accession, was cancelled after the reported difficulties.
The Taiwanese president eventually travelled to Eswatini in May, although details of how he reached the country were not disclosed.
The issue is not limited to Africa, as the US also recognises Beijing but maintains close unofficial ties with Taiwan, including economic, political and defence relations.
That puts Taiwan in an unusual position.
It has strong informal relationships with countries such as the US, but very few formal diplomatic allies, particularly in Africa, where Beijing’s influence has grown significantly over the past decades.
