articles.title_orig: Capitol agenda: Thune plots final votes before midterms
articles.title_zh: Capitol agenda: Thune plots final votes before midterms
articles.content_orig:
Ohio Senate race candidates clash over local energy costs and AI data centers as the 'Fox News Sunday' panel analyzes the upcoming midterm elections. The panel debates the political stakes of high utility bills and Chinese bot farm manipulation on social media. New polling shows a tight Senate race in Maine.
It’s a calculation by Republicans to keep the Senate in session this week.
Yes. The Senate was scheduled to meet anyway over the next few days. But the general consensus early last week was that the Senate would be done then, and those facing competitive races would be back home campaigning.
Republicans wanted to stay in Washington. For a very specific reason. And many of them told Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., as much at their weekly luncheon.
"Odds are we plan on being here next week," said Thune.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS STRUGGLES TO FIND A MESSAGE THAT RESONATES WITH VOTERS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks to reporters outside the chamber at the Capitol in Washington, Thursday, April 2, 2026. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo)
One Senate aide compared the Senate’s schedule to a cat chasing a beam of light from a laser pointer.
But the Senate is in fact meeting. There are reasons. Most of them are political.
The Senate wasn’t quite done with the bill to regulate money in intercollegiate athletics last week. And with the affordability question vexing Republicans, they really didn’t want to pass the college sports bill and promptly vacate Washington. That would be an awkward punctuation point at the end of the legislative sentence before the midterms. GOPers wanted something more substantive. Democrats might have presented that opportunity to Republicans on a platter.
Before the House left for the midterms the week before last, it accentuated its session by passing the Ratepayer Protection Act , 417-3. Let me tell you, not much passes around here with 417 votes. Like their Senate colleagues, House Republicans also worry about voters doubting they’re addressing affordability. So this bill hit the mark for them.
The legislation defrays the costs ratepayers fork out for their utility bills if they’re driven up by data centers. This forces the tech companies which run the data centers to foot the bill.
Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is one of the most vulnerable Republicans on the ballot this fall. Husted’s longtime support for data centers is also dragging him down in the eyes of some voters. Husted tried to fix that. He went to the floor and asked for the Senate to pass on the spot the House bill. However, Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., objected, blocking the effort.
FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE
Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., was one of the key members of the left to help get Sen. Jim Justice's Hershel Woody Williams bill passed unanimously in the Senate. (Elizabeth Frantz)
Republicans viewed that as an opening. Democrats stood in the way of passing a bill on affordability which 417 bipartisan House members supported without blinking. Senate GOPers immediately seized this opportunity as a wedge against their adversaries. And, they interpreted this as a chance to assist their Ohio colleague.
"Tell the data centers we're happy to have you. But you've got to pay your own electricity. People are not going to pay for it," said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La.
Republicans were already leery about the uneven political footing when it comes to AI. Even more so with data centers. Voters are not enamored with the results of the Big, Beautiful Bill, passed last summer. But dealing with data centers is more immediate and might resonate with those who soured on the Republican brand.
"In Missouri, people are absolutely scared to death that these data centers are going to take all the prime farm ground of the state. And then they're going to raise electricity bills so high, no one will be able to afford them," said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo.
The official schedule intended for the Senate to meet this week. But once September hit and no government shutdown loomed, senators from both sides – especially those facing challenging elections – wanted to skip Washington and campaign back home. Yours truly asked Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., why his party stood in the way of the Senate aligning with the House on that data center/utilities measure.
"Was this blocked in the Senate last week by Democrats as an effort to prevent Sen. Husted from having a win in this competitive race?" I asked.
" Sen. Husted's bill is a fraud. It's voluntary. No company has to do it. The bill we have is mandatory. It is much stronger and is what is needed," replied Schumer.
There is something to Schumer’s argument about how muscular the bill is. The legislation says public utility regulators must only consider a standard for ratepayers. Nothing is required. Thus, there’s wiggle room for tech firms.
HAWLEY TAKES AIM AT 'CORPORATE WELFARE' AFTER GOP-BACKED TAX BREAK BOOSTED CONTROVERSIAL INDUSTRY
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat from New York, speaks during a news conference following Senate Democratic policy luncheons at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"What we're saying is that we can do much better," said Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. "Is it a little step forward? Yes. But it's not meeting the moment. So our view is we should expand it to make sure that ratepayers aren't having to subsidize the richest corporations on the planet."
But a lot of Republicans aren’t buying what Schumer and Van Hollen are saying. The Democratic objections are all about three things: Politics. An endangered GOP senator in the most expensive Senate contest in the country. And, Democrats are hoping to flip the seat in their favor.
"Sen. Schumer, what he cares about is the midterm election and politics. And I don't think he cares about the substance of this," said Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas. "Obviously there's a hot and heavy Senate race going on in Ohio, and he doesn't want to let Sen. Husted have something he can talk about when he goes home."
Republicans view the opportunity to turn the affordability issue against Democrats – capitalizing on Schumer’s remark and forcing Democrats to take a stand. Either you’re for affordability (especially as it pertains to the toxic issue of data centers) or you’re not. Moreover, this could boost Husted in his competitive contest with former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio . In fact, it was the Senate GOP’s campaign arm which specifically flagged vulnerabilities for Republicans generally and Husted in particular over the summer.
Thune tees up a test vote on Wednesday to dare Democrats to either start debate on the bill or block it again. That vote requires 60 yeas. So Democratic cooperation is required. Although there’s skepticism anything happens, some Democrats may vote for it. That means the Senate is on the bill. And it’s open to debate and amendments. Thune would have to forge a bipartisan time agreement to finish the measure quickly.
Otherwise – by the book – this would drag into the weekend. And no one wants that. Especially Republicans with competitive races.
12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and the GOP are gearing up for a floor battle with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Senate Democrats over Trump-backed voter ID legislation. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Thune and Schumer want senators back home campaigning. If Democrats impede the legislation Wednesday, the Senate might hang around Thursday or that’s it until after the midterms. Regardless, Republicans will have engineered a vote which they can boomerang against Democrats. Or, at least help Husted and send him back to the Buckeye State with a win.

articles.title_orig: Madonna’s ‘Danceteria’ Was One of the Great Moments in VMAs History
articles.title_zh: Madonna’s ‘Danceteria’ Was One of the Great Moments in VMAs History
articles.content_orig:
Madonna made her big return to the MTV Video Music Awards, her first time at the annual event in 23 years. She practically invented this show the first time it aired in 1984, making her infamous debut in her white wedding gown as the scandalous floor-humping bride in “Like a Virgin.” That performance did wonders for her, but even bigger wonders for the VMAs — it’s the moment this event has always aspired to match ever since. It established her as the once and future queen of this show. But strange as it seems, until Sunday night, she hadn’t rocked the VMAs since 2003, when she did an even better version of “Like a Virgin,” in her legendary make-out session with Britney Spears .
So the stakes were high for her hotly anticipated return Sunday night. But her amazing performance with Sabrina Carpenter and Charli XCX stole the show, with a medley of “One Step Away,” “Bring Your Love,” and “Danceteria,” from her recent Confessions II. It wasn’t just the highlight of the night; it was one of the most stunning performances in the entire history of the VMAs, hands down.
It’s fitting that she began with Sabrina, who was just four years old when Madonna smooched Britney, but a quintessential Daughter of the House of Ciccone. “It’s mother,” a voice moaned at the beginning, as Madonna recited her disco catechism. “The dance floor is not a place,” she said. “It’s a threshold. A ritualistic space where movement replaces language.”
#SabrinaCarpenter makes a surprise appearance during #Madonna ’s #VMAs performance. (via CBS/MTV/VMAs) pic.twitter.com/b7UtSqEilT
Wearing a black beret, Sabrina played the piano with Madonna writhing on top of it. They did their Coachella-slaying duet “Bring Your Love,” with Sabrina twisting and crawling in her glitter-spangled black liederhosen. Madonna wrestled with black-clad storm troopers, then got rolled on a gurney through the crowd, until a really confusing interlude where she met a bizarro alien gospel choir in white gowns. (A very Creed touch.)
But the performance really exploded when Charli XCX strutted in for “Danceteria,” as the stage transformed into the famous early-Eighties NYC disco, with the cool girls hanging out in the men’s room. Charli even stroked the bathroom hand dryer — a clever reference to everybody’s favorite scene in Desperately Seeking Susan .
CHARLI XCX PERFORMING ‘DANCETERIA AFTERHOURS’ WITH MADONNA pic.twitter.com/LbLrourkag
The “Danceteria” bathroom was jumping with party people. Over here, Madonna and Charli rocking out. Over there, Sombr posing as a scantily clad black-leather boy. Hey, look — it’s Debi Mazar, years before Goodfellas , just another party girl and Madonna’s coolest club-kid girlfriend, name-checked in the song. (Also, a callback to Debi’s cameo in the “Music” video from Y2K — maybe Madonna’s peak era ever?) Hey, that guy looks like … wait, it is Fab 5 Freddy, also namechecked. Julia Garner, dressed in the “Open Your Heart” black corset and haircut. Tony Ward, from the “Justify My Love” video. The “Boy Toy” belt buckle. Producer Andrew Watt, as Keith Haring. Seth Rogen … wait, really? What the hell is Seth doing here? Who dragged him to a disco? Ah, well — everybody’s welcome here. Anyone can be a star on Madonna’s dance floor. That’s the whole point of the song — as she keeps chanting, “Everybody here is a work of art.”
A clever detail: Lou Reed’s face on the “Danceteria” bathroom wall, the Mick Rock photo from the cover of his 1972 classic Transformer , as they all sang the “doo de doo de doo” hook from “Walk on the Wild Side.” (Watt walked the red carpet in a T-shirt displaying that Lou photo.) Given my unfortunately encyclopedic memory for trashy award shows, I can tell you this was Lou’s first cameo on the VMAs since 2006, when he and Jack White played “White Light/White Heat” with the Raconteurs.
Madonna made it all feel like a musical autobiography for her, doubling as a capsule history of club culture. It summed up where she came from, why she left, why she came to New York, and what she made of the dreams she worked to bring to life. That’s the theme of her excellent album Confessions II . But she packed the whole messy story into “Danceteria.” Related Content The VMAs: The One Night When MTV Pretends to be MTV Taylor Swift Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton While Accepting Video of the Year Award at 2026 VMAs GENER8ION and Yung Lean Premiere Electrifying Performance of ‘Storm II’ at 2026 VMAs Raye, Sombr, Teddy Swims, Adam Lambert Salute  George Michael at MTV VMAs
Madonna kept winning awards all night, giving magnificently chaotic, unprepared, and awkward speeches, yet still with more star power than anyone in the room. Her best moment: When she won the Best Dance category, she threw her arms around Charli and Troye Sivan and said, “I’m kind of unclear what this award is for?” You and us both, Madonna. Charli had to reread the envelope to confirm it was for her Confessions II short film. She complained about the mic stand being too high for her. She also did one of the most uncomfortable dad jokes ever heard on an award show, including the ones hosted by Billy Crystal: “First of all, I’d like to thank my fingers, because I can always count on them.” Why in God’s name did she say this? Madonna, you’re on live TV here. Hold it together. We’re rooting for you.
But even when she was making everyone squirm (poor Troye looked terrified), she was still the coolest, and she knew it, fully confident this was her show. She told the story of her 1984 “Like a Virgin” moment, and how her management team told her backstage that she’d just killed her career. “My dress went up, and my butt cheek was hanging out,” she recalled. “And in those days, butt cheeks were not hanging out.” When she and Sabrina won for Best Collaboration with “Bring Your Love,” she complained about how Sabrina’s handlers waited to return her call, until Sabrina got bleeped for quipping, “My team is shitting themselves backstage.” But she generously spent her speech heaping praise on Sabrina. “She has OCD and so do I,” Madonna said. “We write our lyrics down on pieces of paper, like they did in the 1800s.” Sabrina simply said, “Everybody, Madonna,” before they walked off hand in hand. THIS DUO!!! @Madonna and @SabrinaAnnLynn take home Best Collaboration at the #VMAs 👯‍♀️🏆 pic.twitter.com/YMlwumHuTd
But the most poignant moment came when Madonna recalled where songs like “Danceteria” came from. “I came to New York to be a dancer,” she said. “Dance is where everything happened for me in my life. I came to life on the dance floor. I found my community on the dance floor. I fell in love with people on the dance floor. And I lost many people I loved on the dance floor.” It was a powerful confession. “Dance brings everybody together, OK?” she said. “We are all equal on the dance floor.” You couldn’t ask for a more succinct summary of everything Madonna’s VMAs performance — or her entire career — has been about.
I’ve been a Madonna fan — and an MTV junkie — since the early days. I’ve seen every VMAs from the beginning, since the night she debuted with “Like a Virgin,” rolling on the floor in her bridal gown, with her rosary beads and Boy Toy belt buckle. So I’m used to seeing Madonna steal the show, year after year — with her glam “Express Yourself” in 1989, her Marie Antoinette-style “Vogue” in 1990, her “Ray of Light” with Lenny Kravitz in 1998. Not to mention her infamously rowdy rooftop interview at the 1995 VMAs, throwing shade with Courtney Love and Kurt Loder. Give Madonna a few minutes of live MTV and she’ll always find a way to seize the moment. articles.content_orig:
People living on the northern Pacific coast of Mexico are bracing for the arrival of Hurricane Polo, which is forecast to make landfall later on Monday or early on Tuesday.
The category three storm, with maximum sustained winds near 115 mph (185 km/h), is expected to move over the state of Baja California Sur, a region popular with tourists and home to the resort destination of Los Cabos.
Meteorologists at the US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) have warned of heavy rainfall which could lead to life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.
Residents on Sunday stocked up on essentials such as drinking water and food as the storm approached.
The NHC warned of the storm surge Hurricane Polo could unleash, which it said could be accompanied by large and destructive waves.
In Cabo San Lucas, famous for its natural rock arch, the authorities restricted access to the beaches. Some restaurants also closed in the town, which acts as a base for sport fishers and whale watchers.
The regional government of Baja California Sur has ordered schools to remain closed on Monday as a preventive measure.
Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío said temporary shelters had been opened should residents need to be evacuated.
The federal authorities have also deployed thousands of members of the navy and the army along with specialised machinery.
Polo has been slowly moving towards Mexico's coast line.
Meteorologists said it was being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon.
